subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

section_titles: Fun at Vegetable Market — comparing weights
periods.activity_title: Heaviest to Lightest: Comparing Weights Around Us

tasks_in_class.description: Look at pictures of animals and write their names from heaviest to lightest.
Write the name of the heaviest object in your home and explain how you know.
What is your weight? How did you know? Write your answer.
What do you think will be the weight of the half pumpkin? Write your estimate.

time_bands.activity: Open with a brief whole-class conversation: ask children to think of the heaviest and lightest living things they have seen. Then move to Opening Q1 (p.115) ("look at pictures of animals and write their names from heaviest to lightest....") — children write their ordered list individually.

Children work on Opening Q2 (p.115) ("write the name of the heaviest object in your home and explain how you know...."). A few volunteers share and the class discusses how they decided — lifting, seeing someone struggle, reading a label. Then Opening Q5 (p.115) ("what is your weight? how did you know?...") follows as a quick written response, with a short pair-share on how weight is found.

Bring the vegetable market scene into focus. Children look at the scale image in Fun at Vegetable Market (p.115) ("what do you think will be the weight of the half pumpkin?...") and write their estimate. Pairs compare estimates and discuss their reasoning; a few share aloud.

Whole-class closing: teacher asks 'What helped you decide which is heavier — looking, lifting, or something else?' Children name the ideas they used. Additional practice: Opening Q3 and Q4, p.115 may be used as paired sharing or brief written tasks at the teacher's discretion.

periods.teacher_notes: Children at this stage compare weights through lived experience — lifting, seeing effort, reading labels — rather than formal measurement, so accept all well-reasoned estimates. A common error is confusing size with weight (a large balloon vs a small stone); invite the class to challenge such reasoning gently. The vegetable market scene grounds the unit in a familiar context that the grams-and-kilograms work ahead will formalise.

section_titles: Kilograms and grams — fractions of a kilogram
periods.activity_title: 500 g, 250 g, 100 g: Building Fractions of a Kilogram

tasks_in_class.description: Estimate the weight of 6 bananas, 5 potatoes, 10 tomatoes, 15 onions as less/more than 1 kg; verify using a weighing balance.
Look at pictures: 2×500g=1kg so 500g=½kg; 4×250g=1kg so 250g=¼kg; 10×100g=1kg. Try doing the same with actual packets.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the vocabulary 'grams' and '1 kilogram = 1000 grams' briefly on the board. Children open to Let Us Do (p.116) ("estimate the weight of 6 bananas, 5 potatoes, 10 tomatoes, 15 onions as less/more than 1 kg...."). In small groups, each group estimates all four items and records their predictions before any weighing.

Groups rotate to the weighing balance (if available) or the teacher demonstrates with the balance at the front, placing produce items to verify estimates. Children update their tables and notice which estimates were surprising. Teacher asks: 'How far off was your estimate, and which way?'

Children move to Let Us Explore Q1 (a)(b)(c) (p.116–117) ("look at pictures: 2×500g=1kg so 500g=½kg; 4×250g=1kg so 250g=¼kg; 10×100g=1kg...."). Teacher uses the pan-balance pictures to lead an inductive build: 'Two of these balance one kilogram — so each is what fraction of a kilogram?' Children complete the sentences and, if packets are available, verify physically.
Quick oral round: teacher holds up fingers (2, 4, 10) and children call out the corresponding fraction (½, ¼, 1/10). This consolidates the three relationships before the class moves to applying them.

periods.teacher_notes: The pan-balance pictures are the conceptual anchor here — children see equivalence before they name fractions, so let them articulate '2 of these equal 1 whole' before writing ½. A common error is writing '500 g = ½' without the unit; reinforce 'half of a kilogram' in full at each step. If a weighing balance is unavailable, 500 g, 250 g, and 100 g packets (or improvised weights in sealed bags) give children the tactile confirmation the section intends.
materials: 500 g, 250 g, 100 g packets or improvised weights
Produce: bananas, potatoes, tomatoes, onions (or pictures)

section_titles: Comparing weights — pan balance and unit matching
periods.activity_title: Erasers, Packets, and Pan Balances: Reasoning with Grams

tasks_in_class.description: How many 250 g packets balance one 500 g packet? Draw packets on the empty pan; complete: 250 g = ___ of 500 g.
Draw arrows to indicate which side the pan balance will tilt for each of the four pictures (a–d).
Match objects (baby, eraser, pen, books, table, fridge, etc.) to the units kilogram or grams.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Think Q1–Q4 (Boxes of Sweet), p.119
tasks_in_class.description: How many boxes of 500 g, 250 g, 100 g, and 50 g each are needed to pack 1 kg Kaju-katli? Write the number for each customer.

homework.description: How many erasers (each 10 g) will weigh the same as a 50 g Haldi packet?

time_bands.activity: Children open to Let Us Find Q1 (p.117) ("how many 250 g packets balance one 500 g packet? draw packets on the empty pan...."). They draw the packets and complete the fraction sentence. Teacher invites one child to explain why two 250 g packets balance — linking back to the gram-fraction relationships children built earlier.

Let Us Find Q2 (p.118) ("draw arrows to indicate which side the pan balance will tilt for each of the four pictures...."). Children work individually, then compare with a partner and resolve any disagreement. Teacher uses Q2 to surface reasoning: 'How do you know that side is heavier without weighing?'

Let Us Find Q3 (p.118) ("match objects — baby, eraser, pen, books, table, fridge — to the units kilogram or grams...."). Teacher does the first example as a think-aloud, then children complete the matching. Brief class check follows.

Let Us Think Q1–Q4 — Boxes of Sweet (p.119) ("how many boxes of 500 g, 250 g, 100 g, and 50 g each are needed to pack 1 kg Kaju-katli?..."). Children work in pairs on each customer's order. Teacher circulates and asks: 'How did you figure out how many boxes?' Additional eraser-weight practice: Let Us Do Q2–Q3, p.119 can be assigned by the teacher as classwork or take-home practice.

periods.teacher_notes: The eraser-as-unit tasks (Let Us Do Q1–Q3, p.119) all share the same procedure — dividing a gram quantity by 10 — so only the richest instance is featured in class; Q2 and Q3 are noted for additional practice at the teacher's discretion. A common error in the Boxes of Sweet task is answering 2 boxes for both the 500 g and 250 g customers without reasoning through the fraction; ask children to show their working in words before writing the number.

section_titles: Weighing machines and real-life weight estimation
periods.activity_title: Lift, Estimate, Convert: Weight in Everyday Life

tasks_in_class.description: Lift objects around you; write names of three you can lift easily and estimate their weights.
How many 1 kg packets are in 10 kg, 20 kg, 50 kg, and 25 kg? Write the answers.
Match objects (cat, elephant, 1-litre bottle, tiger, gas cylinder, pen, leaf, wooden chair) with estimated weight ranges.

homework.description: Ask your parents: find the weight of atta, rice, pulses, and sugar consumed at home in a month; fill the table.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly shows or describes the weighing machine types on p.120 (pan balance, baby scale, kitchen scale, bathroom scale, luggage scale) and asks: 'Which have you seen at home or at a shop?' Children share. Then Let Us Do Q1 (p.121) ("lift objects around you; write names of three you can lift easily and estimate their weights....") — children stand, lift two or three safe classroom objects (book, pencil box, bag), and record their estimates.

Let Us Do Q2 (p.121) — objects lifted with effort — is handled as a brief discussion rather than a separate writing task, folding into the Q1 conversation so both easy and heavy objects are compared. Children note one heavy item they have tried to lift and estimate its weight.

Let Us Do Q3 (a–d) (p.121) ("how many 1 kg packets are in 10 kg, 20 kg, 50 kg, and 25 kg?..."). Children work individually on all four parts. Teacher then reviews: 'If 1 bag holds 1 kg, how many bags do we need for the whole sack?' A quick show-of-slates or fingers check follows.

Let Us Do Q4 (p.121) ("match objects — cat, elephant, 1-litre bottle, tiger, gas cylinder, pen, leaf, wooden chair — with estimated weight ranges...."). Children complete the matching. Teacher selects two or three surprising items (e.g. gas cylinder vs wooden chair) for a brief reasoning conversation: 'How did you decide?' Additional exploration: Let Us Do (monthly consumption), p.120 is set as a home inquiry task.

periods.teacher_notes: The monthly consumption table (p.120) requires a family conversation and is best placed as a home inquiry; a child who cannot access this information may estimate from memory or ask a neighbour. A common error in the kg-to-packets conversion is multiplying instead of recognising that 10 kg simply equals 10 packets of 1 kg — keep the language concrete ('one bag, one kilogram') to prevent abstract confusion. Q2 (lifting with effort) is folded into the Q1 discussion here to avoid repetition, since both tasks share the same estimation act.
materials: Classroom objects of varied weight (books, pencil box, bag)

section_titles: Measuring capacity — litre, millilitre, and fractions
periods.activity_title: Pouring and Estimating: Litres, Millilitres, and Fractions

tasks_in_class.description: Find bottles/containers that hold less than 1 litre, exactly 1 litre, and more than 1 litre; write their names in the table.
How many 500 ml, 250 ml, 100 ml bottles fill a 1 l bottle? How many 250 ml in ½ l and 750 ml? How many 100 ml in ½ l and 800 ml?
Mr Krishna has 1 l perfumed oil; how many bottles of 500 ml, 200 ml, 100 ml, and 50 ml does each customer get?

time_bands.activity: Teacher establishes the parallel: 'We measured weight in grams and kilograms; now we measure liquids in millilitres and litres.' Children look at their classroom or bag for containers they can identify. Measuring Capacity table (p.122) ("find bottles/containers that hold less than 1 litre, exactly 1 litre, and more than 1 litre; write their names....") — children list containers from memory or from items they have brought, filling each column.

Let Us Find (a)(b)(c)(d) (p.123–124) ("how many 500 ml, 250 ml, 100 ml bottles fill a 1 l bottle?..."). Teacher pours or demonstrates with available containers, or uses the book's pictures. Children complete each sub-question and the teacher builds the parallel list on the board: 2×500 ml = 1 l, so 500 ml = ½ l; 4×250 ml = 1 l, so 250 ml = ¼ l; 10×100 ml = 1 l. Children articulate each fraction in words before writing the symbol.

Let Us Do Q4 (a–d) (p.125) ("Mr Krishna has 1 l perfumed oil; how many bottles of 500 ml, 200 ml, 100 ml, and 50 ml does each customer get?..."). Children work in pairs. Teacher asks: 'How is this like the Kaju-katli packing task? What is different?' After working, pairs share answers and explain their reasoning.

Quick oral consolidation: teacher says a fraction (½ l, ¼ l, 1/10 l) and children call out the millilitre equivalent. Additional practice: Let Us Do Q1–Q3 and Q5, p.124–125 and Let Us Explore, p.125 can be assigned by the teacher for classwork or home exploration.

periods.teacher_notes: The pouring activities (T-23, T-24, T-27, T-28) are rich hands-on explorations noted here for additional practice; selecting Q4 in class ensures children meet a cognitively complete problem before the exploration tasks. A common error is confusing litres and millilitres by treating them as interchangeable — reinforce: '1000 millilitres make 1 litre, just as 1000 grams make 1 kilogram.' If measuring containers are unavailable, the book's pictures carry the conceptual work for Let Us Find.
materials: 1 l bottle, 500 ml bottle, 250 ml bottle, 100 ml bottle (if available)

section_titles: Measuring capacity — litre, millilitre, and fractions
Water use, conservation, and measuring containers
periods.activity_title: Small Drops to Big Litres: Measuring and Conserving Water

tasks_in_class.description: Find out how much of these liquids are used at a time: eye drops, honey, cough syrup, cooking oil, and one more.
How many litres of water do you drink daily? How much can a crow drink? How much milk do you drink? How much does an elephant drink?
How much water is used in: shower, watering crops, watering plants, washing clothes, and two more activities? Fill the table using given quantities.
Put a container under a leaking tap for one hour; measure how much water is lost; calculate loss in a day and a week.

time_bands.activity: Children open to Let Us Do Q3 (a–e) (p.124) ("find out how much of these liquids are used at a time: eye drops, honey, cough syrup, cooking oil, and one more...."). Working in pairs, children discuss what they know about small liquid quantities — a drop, a spoonful, a cupful. The teacher draws out that some liquids are measured in single-digit millilitres while others fill hundreds.

Transition to water and its quantities. Let Us Find (a–d) (p.126) ("how many litres of water do you drink daily? how much can a crow drink? how much milk do you drink? how much does an elephant drink?..."). Children write their answers; the class compares human vs animal quantities and discusses the enormous range — from a crow's sip to an elephant's daily need.

Let Us Find activities table (p.126) ("how much water is used in: shower, watering crops, watering plants, washing clothes, and two more activities?..."). Children fill in the table using the given quantities in the book. Teacher guides a brief discussion: 'Which activity uses the most? Does that surprise you?'

Water Conservation activity (p.127) ("put a container under a leaking tap for one hour; measure how much water is lost; calculate loss in a day and a week...."). If a dripping tap is accessible on the school premises, a small group collects water during a break and brings the container; otherwise the teacher provides a sample amount (e.g. 200 ml) as the 'one-hour collection'. Children calculate: if 200 ml drips in one hour, how much in a day (24 hours)? In a week? The class works through the multiplication together.

periods.teacher_notes: The water conservation calculation connects millilitre measurement to multiplication — multiplying an hourly amount by 24 and then by 7 — so children who need support can use repeated addition. A common error is forgetting to convert: children may state the weekly loss in ml when the answer calls for litres, or vice versa; prompt them to check the unit at each step. The small-quantities task (Q3, p.124) brings the capacity section to a close by grounding millilitres in familiar household liquids before moving to the large-scale water contexts of the conservation section.
materials: Container for water collection (cup or bowl)
Access to a dripping or poured-water source

section_titles: Water use, conservation, and measuring containers
periods.activity_title: Milk Cans, Water Use, and Sharing What We Found

tasks_in_class.description: How many litres of water do you drink daily? How much can a crow drink? How much milk do you drink? How much does an elephant drink?
How much water is used in: shower, watering crops, watering plants, washing clothes, and two more activities? Fill the table using given quantities.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces standard milk-measuring cans (50 ml to 1000 ml) from p.127 as familiar capacity-measuring tools. Children look at the scale illustrated and identify markings. A quick question round: 'If I pour two 500 ml cans into a bucket, how much do I have?' Children answer and the class connects the milk-can markings to the fraction relationships built in the capacity section — 500 ml, 250 ml, 100 ml as portions of 1 litre.

Let Us Find (a–d) (p.126) ("how many litres of water do you drink daily? how much can a crow drink? how much milk do you drink? how much does an elephant drink?...") is revisited as a consolidation activity with a fresh lens: children who have gathered information at home share their figures; the class compares and reasons about which quantities are realistic. Teacher asks: 'How would you measure a crow's daily drink — which container would you use?'

Let Us Find activities table (p.126) ("how much water is used in: shower, watering crops, watering plants, washing clothes, and two more activities?..."). Children who did not complete the table in the previous unit do so now; those who have it revisit and add two activities of their own choosing. The class shares the two additional activities added and discusses the units used.

Closing whole-chapter reflection: teacher asks two questions aloud — 'Name one thing you measure in grams and one thing you measure in millilitres' and 'Which fraction of a kilogram surprised you most?' Children respond with a show of hands or a quick written word. This brings the weight and capacity strands together as a natural close.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit returns to the water and capacity questions from the conservation activity to give children who did not complete data collection an opportunity to reason from class-level estimates instead. A common error when reading the milk-can scale is misreading the intermediate markings — children may read 750 ml as 700 ml; walk through one reading together before independent work. The closing reflection drawing weight and capacity together is not a formal test but a quick sense-check that helps the teacher see which conversions still feel uncertain.
materials: Milk-measuring cans or pictures of graduated containers (50 ml to 1000 ml)

items.section_title: Kilograms and grams — fractions of a kilogram
items.prompt: A pan balance has 1 kg on one side. Priya wants to balance it using only 500 g packets. How many 500 g packets does she need?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Two 500 g packets equal 1000 g, which is 1 kg.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be confusing 500 g packets with 250 g packets, thinking four are needed.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is applying the 100 g relationship (ten 100 g = 1 kg) to 500 g packets.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be halving 1000 g incorrectly, arriving at 5 instead of 2.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold a strip of paper in half to see two equal halves; stretch: ask how many 250 g packets would also balance 1 kg.

exercise.description: Estimate the weight of 6 bananas, 5 potatoes, 10 tomatoes, 15 onions as less/more than 1 kg; verify using a weighing balance.

items.section_title: Kilograms and grams — fractions of a kilogram
items.prompt: Raju has four 250 g packets of dal. Do they together weigh more than 1 kg, exactly 1 kg, or less than 1 kg? Write your answer and explain how you know.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Exactly 1 kg. Four 250 g packets together make 1000 g, which equals 1 kg.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Four 250 g packets equal 1000 g because 250 × 4 = 1000, and 1000 g = 1 kg.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw four equal boxes and label each 250 g, then add them up; stretch: ask what five 250 g packets would weigh and whether that is more or less than 1 kg.

exercise.description: Look at pictures: 2×500g=1kg so 500g=½kg; 4×250g=1kg so 250g=¼kg; 10×100g=1kg. Try doing the same with actual packets.

items.section_title: Weighing machines and real-life weight estimation
items.prompt: Meena picks up her pencil box and lifts it with ease. She picks up her schoolbag and it feels very heavy. Which object is most likely measured in grams?

options.label: D
options.text: Neither — both are measured in kilograms

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Light everyday objects like a pencil box are measured in grams; heavier objects like a schoolbag are measured in kilograms.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has reversed the unit assignment, placing the heavier item in grams.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has not yet connected effort-to-lift with unit choice.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has over-generalised kilograms to all objects, ignoring small/light items.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student lift a pencil and a book and decide which feels closer to a gram and which to a kilogram; stretch: ask the student to name two more objects — one in grams and one in kilograms — and justify.

exercise.description: Lift objects around you; write names of three you can lift easily and estimate their weights.

items.section_title: Measuring capacity — litre, millilitre, and fractions
items.prompt: A water bottle holds 500 ml. A jug holds 1 litre. If Tara fills the jug using only the water bottle, how many times must she fill and pour the water bottle?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: 500 ml + 500 ml = 1000 ml = 1 litre, so two fills are needed.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be thinking of 250 ml bottles (four of which make 1 litre).
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may be confusing 500 ml with 100 ml, applying the ten-fills relationship.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be dividing 1000 by 200 rather than 500.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw two equal boxes side by side labelled 500 ml each and show them combining to 1000 ml; stretch: ask how many 250 ml cups would fill the same jug.

exercise.description: Find bottles/containers that hold less than 1 litre, exactly 1 litre, and more than 1 litre; write their names in the table.

items.section_title: Measuring capacity — litre, millilitre, and fractions
items.prompt: A bottle holds 250 ml. How many such bottles fill a 1 litre container? How many fill a 750 ml container? Write both answers and explain your thinking.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Four 250 ml bottles fill 1 litre (4 × 250 = 1000 ml = 1 l). Three 250 ml bottles fill 750 ml (3 × 250 = 750 ml).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply 250 ml by the number of bottles and check when the total reaches the target volume.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw and count 250 ml boxes until they reach 1000 ml or 750 ml; stretch: ask how many 250 ml bottles would fill a 1.5 litre bottle.

exercise.description: How many 500 ml, 250 ml, 100 ml bottles fill a 1 l bottle? How many 250 ml in ½ l and 750 ml? How many 100 ml in ½ l and 800 ml?

items.section_title: Water use, conservation, and measuring containers
items.prompt: A leaking tap drips 300 ml of water every hour. How much water is wasted in one full day? Write your answer in millilitres and also write whether this is more or less than 1 litre.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 300 ml × 24 hours = 7200 ml. This is more than 1 litre (since 1 litre = 1000 ml and 7200 ml is much greater).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the hourly drip amount by 24 to find the daily total, then compare with 1000 ml.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: help the student first find how much drips in 2 hours, then 4 hours, building up using repeated addition; stretch: ask how much water would be saved in a week if the tap were fixed.

exercise.description: Put a container under a leaking tap for one hour; measure how much water is lost; calculate loss in a day and a week.

items.section_title: Fun at Vegetable Market — comparing weights
items.prompt: A cow, a rabbit, a horse, and a hen are shown in pictures. Which order lists them from heaviest to lightest?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use knowledge of animal sizes and body mass to order from heaviest to lightest.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has reversed the order, listing from lightest to heaviest.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has swapped horse and cow, suggesting uncertainty about which large animal is heavier.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has listed from lightest to heaviest and also swapped horse and cow.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to first sort into 'big animals' and 'small animals' before ordering within each group; stretch: ask the student to estimate a weight in kilograms for each animal and justify.

exercise.description: Look at pictures of animals and write their names from heaviest to lightest.

items.section_title: Fun at Vegetable Market — comparing weights
items.prompt: A whole watermelon is shown on a weighing scale. The scale shows 4 kg. A seller cuts the watermelon in half. What do you think each half weighs? How do you know?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each half weighs 2 kg. Because the whole watermelon weighs 4 kg and it is cut into two equal halves, each half is 4 ÷ 2 = 2 kg.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total weight equally by 2 since the cut produces two equal halves.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw the watermelon split into two equal parts and label the total; stretch: ask what each piece would weigh if the watermelon were cut into four equal pieces instead.

exercise.description: What do you think will be the weight of the half pumpkin? Write your estimate.

items.section_title: Comparing weights — pan balance and unit matching
items.prompt: One pan of a balance holds a 500 g packet of rice. Anita wants to balance it using only 250 g packets. How many 250 g packets does she need, and what fraction of 500 g is one 250 g packet? Write your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Anita needs 2 packets of 250 g. One 250 g packet is half (½) of 500 g.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Two 250 g packets equal 500 g; so 250 g is ½ of 500 g.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw the two pans and sketch packets until they look balanced; stretch: ask the student what fraction of 1 kg a single 250 g packet represents.

exercise.description: How many 250 g packets balance one 500 g packet? Draw packets on the empty pan; complete: 250 g = ___ of 500 g.

items.section_title: Comparing weights — pan balance and unit matching
items.prompt: Which of these objects would you most likely measure in grams rather than kilograms?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Very light objects like an eraser are measured in grams; heavier objects are measured in kilograms.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not connected the size and weight of large appliances to kilograms.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may not yet appreciate that a standard bag of rice is typically measured in kilograms.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has not yet generalised that human body weight is measured in kilograms.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to hold an eraser and a book — which is closer to what they could weigh on a small kitchen scale in grams? Stretch: name two more objects measured in grams and two in kilograms.

exercise.description: Match objects (baby, eraser, pen, books, table, fridge, etc.) to the units kilogram or grams.

items.section_title: Comparing weights — pan balance and unit matching
items.prompt: A sweet shop has 1 kg of Kaju-katli. Customer A wants a 500 g box and Customer B wants a 250 g box. How many boxes does each customer get? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Customer A gets 2 boxes of 500 g (2 × 500 g = 1000 g = 1 kg). Customer B gets 4 boxes of 250 g (4 × 250 g = 1000 g = 1 kg).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide 1000 g by the box size: 1000 ÷ 500 = 2 for Customer A, 1000 ÷ 250 = 4 for Customer B.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw a 1 kg bar and shade 500 g sections for A and 250 g sections for B; stretch: ask how many 100 g boxes a third customer would need.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Think Q1–Q4 (Boxes of Sweet), p.119
exercise.description: How many boxes of 500 g, 250 g, 100 g, and 50 g each are needed to pack 1 kg Kaju-katli? Write the number for each customer.

items.section_title: Weighing machines and real-life weight estimation
items.prompt: Which of these animals is most likely to have a weight in the range of 3 to 5 kg?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: A typical house cat weighs between 3 and 5 kg; the other options are far heavier.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not connected elephant size to very large weight (thousands of kg).
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is estimating a wooden chair as very light, not recognising it is typically heavier than a cat.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has not recognised that a tiger is much heavier than 3–5 kg.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to think of how heavy a cat feels when held, then compare that feeling to lifting a chair or imagining an elephant; stretch: ask the student to estimate the weight range for a tiger in kg.

exercise.description: Match objects (cat, elephant, 1-litre bottle, tiger, gas cylinder, pen, leaf, wooden chair) with estimated weight ranges.

items.section_title: Measuring capacity — litre, millilitre, and fractions
items.prompt: A doctor prescribes 5 ml of cough syrup to be taken at a time. A bottle contains 100 ml. How many doses are in the bottle? Is this amount of cough syrup closer to a teaspoon or to a full glass of water?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 100 ÷ 5 = 20 doses. Each 5 ml dose is closer to a teaspoon (a teaspoon holds roughly 5 ml), not a full glass.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total volume by the dose size; compare 5 ml with familiar small containers.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to count by 5s from 0 to 100 and count the steps; stretch: ask how many days the bottle lasts if one dose is taken morning and evening each day.

exercise.description: Find out how much of these liquids are used at a time: eye drops, honey, cough syrup, cooking oil, and one more.

items.section_title: Water use, conservation, and measuring containers
items.prompt: Ravi says he drinks about 2 litres of water every day. His younger sister drinks about 1 litre. Together, how many litres do they drink in 3 days? Is this more or less than 10 litres?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Together they drink 2 + 1 = 3 litres per day. In 3 days: 3 × 3 = 9 litres. This is less than 10 litres.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add daily totals first, then multiply by the number of days, and compare with 10.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw one day's water as two bottles (Ravi) and one bottle (sister) and count the total before multiplying; stretch: ask how many days it would take for both together to drink exactly 15 litres.

exercise.description: How much water is used in: shower, watering crops, watering plants, washing clothes, and two more activities? Fill the table using given quantities.

items.section_title: Weighing machines and real-life weight estimation
items.prompt: A sack of wheat weighs 25 kg. How many 1 kg packets can be filled from this sack?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Each packet holds 1 kg, so the number of packets equals the total weight in kg: 25 kg ÷ 1 kg = 25.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to count on from 1 kg to 25 kg, marking each step as one packet; stretch: ask how many packets could be filled from a 50 kg sack and whether the answer doubles.

exercise.description: How many 1 kg packets are in 10 kg, 20 kg, 50 kg, and 25 kg? Write the answers.

items.section_title: Measuring capacity — litre, millilitre, and fractions
items.prompt: Mrs Sita has 1 litre of cooking oil. She wants to fill small bottles of 200 ml each. How many bottles can she fill completely?

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student count by 200s — 200, 400, 600, 800, 1000 — and count the steps; stretch: ask how much oil would remain if she filled 4 bottles and what fraction of a bottle that leftover is.

exercise.description: Mr Krishna has 1 l perfumed oil; how many bottles of 500 ml, 200 ml, 100 ml, and 50 ml does each customer get?
